```{python}
        point_to(fld, p, (-3.8, 13.5), (0.5, 8.6), "Y and Z cross\nbehind H: traffic", fontsize=6.4, color=OD)
    elif variant == "snag":
        route_to(p, "Z", (4.6, 13.0), (5.0, 9.8))
        route_to(p, "H", (4.6, 8.5), (9.6, 15.0))
        route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 5.5), (0.8, 15.6))
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=lat, window=win)
        tri = [(5.0, 9.8), (9.6, 15.0), (0.8, 15.6), (5.0, 9.8)]
        xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in tri]), np.array([q[1] for q in tri]))
        ax.fill(xs, ys, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.12, zorder=1.7)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=READ_GREEN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=1.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.0, 11.4, "shaded: 3 receivers\nv 2 defenders", fontsize=6.3, color=READ_GREEN)
    elif variant == "sprint":
        move_to(p, "QB", (-5.5, 2.6), (-4.6, 6.0), (-3.4, 8.0), kind="run")
        move_to(p, "RB", (-3.8, 3.0), (-1.6, 3.6), kind="block")                 # stays in: inside protection
        move_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 6.0), kind="block")                                 # seals the end inside
        route_to(p, "Z", (2.6, 13.6), (9.4, 13.0))                                # clears the corner
        route_to(p, "H", (1.0, 12.0), (1.6, 15.0))                                # the end-zone flat
        p.highlight("NB")
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=lat, window=win)
        branch(fld, p, [(-3.4, 8.0), (-1.4, 8.6), (2.2, 8.8)], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.6)
        point_to(fld, p, (8.8, 9.4), (2.6, 10.6), "flat defender:\nH or the QB?", fontsize=6.4, color=READ_GREEN)
    else:
        move_to(p, "QB", (-4.0, 0.6), (-2.4, 3.2), (-0.6, 4.6), (1.4, 4.9), (3.6, 4.9), kind="run")
        move_to(p, "RB", (-3.2, 4.6), (0.0, 6.1), kind="block")                 # kicks out the end
        move_to(p, "LG", (-1.6, -1.4), (-1.6, 2.6), (0.2, 4.2), (2.6, 2.0), kind="pull")   # leads for the Mike
        move_to(p, "C", (0.2, -0.5), kind="block")                               # back on the backside tackle
        move_to(p, "LT", (-1.2, -3.4), kind="block")                             # hinge
        move_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 1.2), (2.8, -2.6), kind="block")                  # climbs to the backside Will
        move_to(p, "RT", (0.3, 2.7), kind="block")                               # down on the 3-technique
        move_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 3.4), kind="block")                                # down, with the tackle
        move_to(p, "H", (1.6, 10.4), kind="block")
        move_to(p, "Z", (3.0, 14.4), kind="block")
        p.highlight("QB")
        p.highlight("LG", color=style.SERIES[6])
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=lat, window=win)
        branch(fld, p, [(LINE_D, -1.6), (-1.6, -1.4), (-1.6, 2.6), (0.2, 4.2), (2.6, 2.0)], color=style.SERIES[6],
               lw=2.0, dash="-", z=4.5)
        say(fld, p, -4.4, 11.6, "the back blocks:\n10 blockers, 1 runner", fontsize=6.4, color=OD)
    panel_title(ax, title, fs=8.2)
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.2))
tp_panel(axes[0, 0], "bunch", "A  Bunch rub (vs man)")
tp_panel(axes[0, 1], "snag", "B  Snag triangle (vs zone)")
tp_panel(axes[1, 0], "sprint", "C  Sprint-out option")
tp_panel(axes[1, 1], "power", "D  QB power")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4, w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Each shape answers a defensive call. Against the man coverage that dominates the goal line, the bunch rub
(A) is the classic: three receivers starting close together, two crossing just behind the third, and three
defenders who must either fight through traffic or switch assignments perfectly. Against zone, the
[snag](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd) triangle (B), from Quick Game (the snag itself is a
receiver who runs five yards and sits down facing the quarterback), puts three receivers in one area guarded
by two defenders: whichever receiver the defenders leave, the quarterback throws to. The sprint-out option (C) doesn't care much which coverage it gets,
because it attacks one defender with two threats. And the quarterback run (D), the extra-hat idea from
[Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd), gives the offense one more blocker than a
handoff can, which matters most when two yards is all it needs.

Notice what's missing: deep routes, long developing reads, anything that needs a second and a half to come
open. From the 2 the end line is 12 yards away, and a pass rush arrives in about two and a half seconds.
Two-point plays are designed to be decided by the quarterback's first look.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New England, Super Bowl LI (2016 season)"}
Down 28–3 in the third quarter against Atlanta, the Patriots needed two two-point conversions just to tie,
and got both. The first, after Danny Amendola's touchdown catch made it 28–18 with about six minutes left,
was a [direct snap](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) to running back
James White: Brady stood in the shotgun, White motioned in beside him, the center snapped the ball straight
to White, and he ran it up the middle for 28–20. The second, after
White's own 1-yard touchdown run with 57 seconds left, was a quick throw from Tom Brady to Amendola for
28–28. New England won in overtime, 34–28.[^li] **What to notice:** two different answers on the same night,
a run with the quarterback out of the play and a quick pass; a defense that had seen one couldn't sit on it
the next time. Why take the quarterback out of a run, when this chapter keeps saying a running quarterback
adds a blocker? Because Brady was never a running threat, so the extra-hat arithmetic didn't apply to him.
What the direct snap bought was speed and surprise: the ball went straight to the runner, with no handoff,
against a defense set up to stop a Brady pass.
:::

## Goal-line personnel: the biggest people on the field

Inside the 3 or so, both teams change their players. The offense brings in its heaviest
[personnel](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd): two or three tight ends, a
fullback, sometimes a sixth offensive lineman (a
[jumbo](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) package) who has to
[report as eligible](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd): tell the
referee, who announces it, because a lineman's number normally makes him an ineligible receiver. And
sometimes the extra body is a defensive
lineman playing fullback. The most famous of those was William "The Refrigerator" Perry, the Chicago Bears'
rookie defensive tackle, who scored a 1-yard touchdown in Super Bowl XX in January 1986.[^fridge] The idea is
simple arithmetic: every receiver taken off the field is replaced by a blocker, so the offense can match
the defense body for body near the ball.

The defense answers in kind with a [**goal-line defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-goal-line-defense):
extra linemen and linebackers in place of defensive backs, everyone lined up close to the ball, every gap
along the line filled before the snap. The two classic shapes are the **6-2** (six down linemen, two
linebackers, three defensive backs) and the **5-3** (five down linemen, three linebackers, three defensive
backs). Both put eight defenders within about three yards of the ball.

Why two shapes? Against an offense with a tight end at each end of the line there are eight gaps to fill
(A, B, C and D on each side, from
[The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd)). The 6-2 puts six of those eight defenders on the line, in the gaps, low, and lets the two
linebackers fill the last two: it is the stronger shape right at the ball, built to win the first yard by
force. The 5-3 takes one lineman off the line and adds a third linebacker. It gives up a little of that
force, but it gains a defender standing up, who can see the play, fill whichever gap the run goes to, or
pick up a tight end or fullback who slips out for a pass. So the 6-2 suits the last yard against an
offense that just pounds the ball, and the 5-3 suits a defense that fears play-action from the same look.

```{python}
#| label: fig-goalline-fronts
#| fig-cap: "Goal-line personnel on both sides, ball on the 1. The offense is in 23 personnel (a fullback F and a running back R, plus three tight ends: Y and U on the line and H as a wing just outside Y), with tight line splits. Left, a 6-2 goal-line defense: six linemen in the gaps along the line, low, the two linebackers filling the last two gaps, and three defensive backs for the tight ends and the wing. Right, a 5-3: a nose tackle (N) on the center, four more linemen, three linebackers. Both fill every gap from tight end to tight end at the snap. The defenders' letters show their usual positions; on goal-line snaps the labels matter less than the gaps."
def jumbo():
    return line5(split=1.55) + [O("QB", "QB", -2.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.2, 0.0, "F"),
                                 O("RB", "RB", -6.4, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.65),
                                 O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.65, "U"), O("W", "TE", -2.0, 6.3, "H")]


def gl_panel(ax, kind):
    if kind == "62":
        dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -6.0, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -3.9, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.85, "T"),
               D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.85, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 3.9, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 6.3, "E"),
               D("LB1", "LB", 2.8, -2.3, "M"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.8, 2.3, "W"),
               D("CB1", "CB", 2.4, -8.2, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 2.6, 8.4, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.6, "SS")]
        notes = [("6 linemen +\n2 LBs: 8 gaps", (-4.6, -7.0))]
    else:
        dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -5.3, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -2.3, "T"), D("N", "NT", 0.9, 0.0, "N"),
               D("T2", "DT", 0.9, 2.3, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 5.5, "E"),
               D("LB1", "LB", 2.8, -3.6, "W"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.8, 0.0, "M"), D("LB3", "LB", 2.8, 3.8, "S"),
               D("CB1", "CB", 2.4, -8.2, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 2.6, 8.4, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -1.9, "SS")]
        notes = [("5 linemen,\n3 linebackers", (-4.6, -7.0))]
    p = Play(jumbo(), dfn, los=opp(1), to_go=None)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-10.5, 10.5), window=(-8.0, 8.5))
    for text, at in notes:
        say(fld, p, at[0], at[1], text, fontsize=6.6, color=DD)
    say(fld, p, 6.8, -5.0, "end zone", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
    panel_title(ax, "6-2 goal line" if kind == "62" else "5-3 goal line")
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
gl_panel(axes[0], "62")
gl_panel(axes[1], "53")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Football coaches have a three-word rule for this part of the field: **low man wins**. When two big men
collide at the line, the one whose pads are lower gets under the other, lifts him and drives him back. On
an ordinary down that matters; at the goal line it is almost everything, because the play will be decided
within a yard of the ball. So goal-line defensive linemen often line up in four-point stances, both hands
on the ground, and fire *under* the blockers, aiming to knock the offensive line back into the backfield
and create a pile the runner can't cross. Linebackers fill whatever gap is left, often by going over the
top of the pile.

What does the offense run into all that? Mostly the same handful of downhill runs you met in
[Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), and the simplest is the one below:
the [iso](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), a fullback leading into a gap onto the one
linebacker who fills it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-goalline-iso
#| fig-cap: "The run a goal-line defense is built to stop: an iso from the I formation against the 6-2, ball on the 1. The right guard blocks the A-gap tackle down and the right tackle blocks the C-gap tackle out, which opens the right B gap; the fullback (F) leads through it onto the linebacker who fills it (W, ringed), and the running back (R) follows him in, needing only to get the ball across the goal line a yard away. The other linebacker (M) tries to come over the top of the pile. Every other blocker simply fires low into the man in front of him. At the goal line this is low man wins in its purest form: whoever gets lower at the hole wins it."
p = Play(jumbo(), [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -6.0, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -3.9, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.85, "T"),
                   D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.85, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 3.9, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 6.3, "E"),
                   D("LB1", "LB", 2.8, -2.3, "M"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.8, 2.3, "W"),
                   D("CB1", "CB", 2.4, -8.2, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 2.6, 8.4, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.6, "SS")],
         los=opp(1), to_go=None)
move_to(p, "RG", (0.1, 1.0), kind="block")                 # down on the A-gap tackle
move_to(p, "RT", (0.2, 4.2), kind="block")                 # out on the C-gap tackle
for k, w in (("LT", -3.3), ("LG", -1.7), ("C", -0.4)):
    move_to(p, k, (0.1, w), kind="block")
move_to(p, "Y", (0.2, 5.9), kind="block")
move_to(p, "U", (0.2, -5.6), kind="block")
move_to(p, "FB", (-3.0, 0.9), (-0.6, 1.9), (1.5, 2.2), kind="block")    # leads through the B gap onto W
move_to(p, "RB", (-5.0, 1.1), (-2.6, 2.5), (-0.6, 2.7), (0.9, 2.6), kind="run")   # follows him into the hole
p.highlight("LB2")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-10.0, 10.0), window=(-8.0, 7.2))
branch(fld, p, [(2.8, -2.3), (3.1, -0.6), (2.6, 0.9)], color=style.DEFENSE)
point_to(fld, p, (5.2, -4.4), (3.1, -0.8), "M: over the top", fontsize=6.6, color=DD)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.6, 5.4), (-1.8, 1.4), "F leads into\nthe B gap", fontsize=6.6, color=OD)
say(fld, p, 5.4, 7.4, "end zone", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["carrier", "block", "react", "ring"], fs=6.6, ncol=4, y=-0.01)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
A goal-line defense exists because near the goal line the run is a real threat on every snap and the pass
has little room to hurt you. Trading cornerbacks and safeties for linemen and linebackers trades coverage,
which the compressed field has made cheap, for gap control and size, which the last yard has made
precious. **What it gives up:** coverage. Goal-line defenses are built to stop a run up the middle, and
their worst nightmare is the play that looks exactly like that run and isn't: the play-action pass to a
tight end or a fullback slipping out, or a quarterback rollout to the edge where fewer defenders are
standing. That is why, when heavy personnel does throw near the goal line, it almost always fakes the run
first: inside the 3 in 2023–2025, offenses with one wide receiver or none passed on only
`{python} pct(HEAVY_PASS)` of snaps, but `{python} pct(HEAVY_PA)` of those dropbacks were play-action, against
`{python} pct(LIGHT_PA)` from lighter groupings.[^heavy]
:::

## The quarterback sneak

The shortest play in football is the
[**QB sneak**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-sneak). The quarterback takes the snap under center and
immediately drives forward behind his center, usually into one of the gaps beside him, to gain a yard or
less. No handoff, no fake, no read.

It is the most reliable play in the book for one yard, and the reasons are worth spelling out:

- **The ball starts closest to the line.** On a handoff, the ball goes backward to a running back five to
  seven yards deep, who then has to gain all of that back before he gains anything. On a sneak, the ball
  is a foot behind the line when the quarterback has it.
- **It is the fastest play there is.** The ball goes from the center's hands to the quarterback's
  and forward in a fraction of a second, before linebackers can read the play and fill.
- **The quarterback is the extra blocker's dividend.** On every other run, the quarterback hands off and
  stops being a factor; on the sneak he *is* the runner, so every other player can block, the same extra-hat
  arithmetic as QB power.
- **The defense can't see it coming any differently.** A quarterback under center on third-and-1 might
  sneak, hand off, or fake and throw. Defenses have to defend all three.

And its blocking is simple. Coaches call it **wedge** blocking: every lineman drives low and forward toward
the center's hip, so the front moves as one block with no seams for a defender to slip through, often with
the center and a guard double-teaming whoever lines up over the ball. The quarterback's coaching point is
just as simple: follow the center's backside into the first crease. And the
[cadence](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd), the quarterback's call that tells his line when
the ball will be snapped, is a weapon either way. A *quick count* snaps the ball on the first sound, before
the defense has settled into its stances; a
[hard count](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd), a long, loud call with a sudden bark meant to
draw the defense offside, aims for the free yard without snapping it at all.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sneak-vs-push
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to gain a yard, third-and-1, from the same heavy formation: tight ends Y and U on the ends of the line, a wing (H) outside Y, and tight line splits. Left, the classic quarterback sneak: the quarterback (Q) alone under center, a fullback (F) and running back (R) deep, so the defense has to respect a handoff. At the snap the center and guards drive forward and the quarterback follows his center into the nearest crease, here the right A gap, between center and guard. Right, the tush push: the same sneak, but the backs have been replaced by two pushers (P) lined up almost against the quarterback's hips (drawn a little apart here so the letters show), who drive into him at the snap and shove the whole pile forward. The defense, crowding the A gaps, lines up the same way against both. The yellow line is the line to gain, one yard away."
SNEAK_SPLIT = 1.3          # nearly foot to foot: the push line closes its splits


def sneak_off(push, p_d=-2.8):
    """Short-yardage offense: tight splits, tight ends on both ends of the line, the quarterback under center."""
    off = line5(split=SNEAK_SPLIT) + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 3.95),
                                      O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -3.95, "U"), O("W", "TE", -1.7, 5.4, "H")]
    if push:
        off += [O("P1", "RB", p_d, -0.75, "P"), O("P2", "TE", p_d, 0.75, "P")]
    else:
        off += [O("RB", "RB", -6.2, 0.0, "R"), O("FB", "FB", -4.1, 0.0, "F")]
    return off


def short_def():
    """A short-yardage front: six linemen low (two in the A gaps beside the center), three linebackers."""
    return [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -5.4, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -2.3, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.75, "T"),
            D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.75, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 2.3, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 5.4, "E"),
            D("MIKE", "LB", 2.6, -1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 2.6, 1.4, "W"), D("SAM", "LB", 2.3, 6.4, "S"),
            D("CB1", "CB", 3.0, -8.0, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 0.0, "SS")]


def carrier_arrow(fld, p, pts):
    """The ball carrier's path through the pile: drawn over the markers but see-through, so the letters
    it crosses stay readable."""
    xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=OD, lw=2.2, alpha=0.55, zorder=11, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=12,
                                     color=OD, lw=2.2, zorder=11))


def sneak_panel(ax, push):
    p = Play(sneak_off(push, p_d=-3.2), short_def(), los=opp(35), to_go=1)
    for k in ("LG", "C", "RG"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.6, 0.0)])
    if push:
        p.highlight("P1", "P2")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-7.0, 6.5))
    if push:
        carrier_arrow(fld, p, [(-1.9, 0.0), (-0.2, 0.0), (2.0, 0.0), (2.6, 0.0)])
        say(fld, p, -4.9, -4.0, "2 pushers, tight\nbehind the QB", fontsize=6.6, color=READ_GREEN, weight="bold")
    else:
        carrier_arrow(fld, p, [(-1.9, 0.0), (-0.3, 0.4), (2.0, 0.4), (2.6, 0.4)])
        say(fld, p, -3.6, -4.0, "QB alone:\nfollow the center", fontsize=6.6, color=OD)
    panel_title(ax, "Tush push" if push else "Quarterback sneak")
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
sneak_panel(axes[0], False)
sneak_panel(axes[1], True)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Tom Brady (2000–2022) and Josh Allen (2018–2025)"}
Two quarterbacks show the two ways to be a great sneaker. Tom Brady, a 6-foot-4 pocket passer who was never
fast and never needed to be, won with *timing*. Counting every run he made with a yard or less to go,
regular season and playoffs, nflverse play-by-play has Brady carrying `{python} BRADY[0]` times and gaining
the first down or the touchdown on `{python} pct(BRADY[1])` of them; almost all were sneaks.[^qbone] The
Patriots often ran it on a quick count, and Brady was over the center's back before the linebackers had
moved. Josh Allen, one of the biggest and strongest quarterbacks in the league, wins with *size*: he sneaks,
pushes and runs QB power with equal comfort, and Buffalo ran the second-most sneaks of 2022–2025. On every
Allen carry for the Bills with a yard or less to go, nflverse has him converting `{python} pct(ALLEN[1])` of
`{python} ALLEN[0]` tries, essentially level with Brady's career mark.[^qballen] **What to notice:** on old
Patriots film, how *quickly* the ball is snapped; on Bills film, where Allen goes. A pure sneak goes
straight ahead; Allen often bounces a step to the A or B gap where the pile is softest, using his size like
a running back's.
:::

## The tush push

The [**tush push**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tush-push) is a quarterback sneak with help from behind.
Two or three teammates (usually a running back and a tight end, sometimes a third player) line up directly
behind the quarterback, and at the snap they drive into him and push. The offensive line fires low and
forward; the quarterback, crouched behind his center, surges into the line; the pushers add their weight
from behind, and the whole mass moves forward, usually just far enough. Philadelphia fans called it the
Brotherly Shove.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tush-push
#| fig-cap: "The tush push, simulated (BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron, not recorded): third-and-1 at the opponent's 35. 1: the quarterback (ringed) is under center with two pushers (P) directly behind him. 2: at the snap, the offensive line fires low into the defensive linemen before they can rise. 3: the center and right guard drive the two A-gap tackles back and apart, opening a seam between them; the quarterback slides into it and the pushers drive into his back, while the linebackers (M, W) come forward to meet the pile at the top. 4: the pile, still moving as one, carries the ball (brown) more than a yard past the yellow line. The whole play is decided in about a second, and the front of the pile moves only a yard or two. Markers are drawn a little smaller than in the other diagrams so that engaged players stay visible."
def push_play():
    """Keyframes for every body at the snap, first contact, mid-push and the finish. The pile moves as a
    block, so each moment is placed by hand to keep engaged players about a yard and a quarter apart."""
    p = Play(sneak_off(True), short_def(), los=opp(35), to_go=1)
    K = {   # key: [(d, w) at t = 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]
        "LT": [(-0.25, -2.6), (0.05, -2.75), (0.3, -2.85)], "LG": [(-0.15, -1.3), (0.45, -1.5), (0.9, -1.65)],
        "C": [(-0.1, 0.0), (0.55, -0.35), (1.5, -0.75)], "RG": [(-0.15, 1.3), (0.55, 1.5), (1.5, 1.75)],
        "RT": [(-0.25, 2.6), (0.3, 2.8), (0.6, 2.95)], "U": [(-0.4, -3.95), (-0.2, -4.1), (0.0, -4.2)],
        "Y": [(-0.4, 3.95), (-0.2, 4.1), (0.0, 4.2)], "W": [(-1.5, 5.2), (-1.3, 5.1), (-1.1, 5.0)],
        "QB": [(-1.5, 0.05), (0.0, 0.5), (1.6, 0.7)],
        "P1": [(-2.4, -0.6), (-1.0, -0.05), (0.4, 0.05)], "P2": [(-2.4, 0.8), (-1.0, 1.25), (0.4, 1.4)],
        "E1": [(1.0, -5.5), (1.05, -5.55), (1.1, -5.6)], "T1": [(0.95, -2.4), (1.2, -2.6), (1.5, -2.8)],
        "T2": [(0.95, -0.8), (1.6, -1.2), (2.5, -1.7)], "T3": [(0.95, 0.85), (1.6, 1.8), (2.5, 2.6)],
        "T4": [(0.95, 2.4), (1.35, 3.1), (1.8, 3.65)], "E2": [(1.0, 5.6), (1.05, 5.8), (1.1, 5.9)],
        "MIKE": [(2.4, -1.3), (2.9, -0.8), (3.6, -0.3)], "WILL": [(2.4, 1.3), (2.8, 1.0), (3.4, 1.3)],
        "SAM": [(2.3, 6.3), (2.4, 6.1), (2.6, 6.0)], "SS": [(4.8, 0.0), (4.7, 0.2), (4.6, 0.4)],
        "CB1": [(3.0, -8.0), (3.0, -7.8), (3.0, -7.6)],
    }
    tr = {}
    for k, pts in K.items():
        q = p.players[k]
        tr[k] = ease([(0.0, q.d, q.w)] + [(t, d, w) for t, (d, w) in zip((0.4, 0.8, 1.2), pts)])
    set_tracks(p, tr, t_end=1.3)
    return p


def push_ball(t, fld, p):
    """The ball, held out in front of the quarterback once he has it."""
    if t <= 0.05:
        return
    d, w = p.position("QB", t)
    bd = d + 0.75
    x, y = P(fld, p, bd, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 0.55, 0.85, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=12))


PUSH = push_play()
PUSH_T = [0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]
PUSH_N = ["Under center, two pushers\nstacked behind the QB.",
          "Snap: the line fires low into\nthe linemen before they rise.",
          "QB slides in behind the center;\npushers drive into his back.",
          "The pile carries the ball\nwell past the line to gain."]
PUSH_LAT, PUSH_WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-4.6, 5.0)
if PDF:
    strip_grid(PUSH, PUSH_T, PUSH_N, PUSH_LAT, PUSH_WIN, rings=(("QB", style.THIRD),), mr=0.55, deco=push_ball)
    plt.show()
else:
    video(PUSH, PUSH_LAT, PUSH_WIN, 1.3, rings=(("QB", style.THIRD),), notes=PUSH_N, times=PUSH_T,
          t_start=-0.3, mr=0.55, deco=push_ball)
```

Why does a shove from behind help that much? Physics, mostly. A sneak is a pushing contest at the line: the
offense's linemen and quarterback against the defense's linemen and linebackers, both sides trying to move a
pile a yard. Two pushers behind the quarterback add a few hundred pounds of driving force at exactly the
point of the contest, and they add it *immediately*, at the snap, before the defense's second level can
arrive. The defense can't add the same force, because its extra bodies have to come from the other side of
a pile they can't get into. And the quarterback, pushed from behind, can stay low and keep his feet driving
instead of being stopped upright by the first linebacker to hit him.

Notice what the push gives up. A plain sneak hides inside a formation that could also hand off or throw;
the push announces itself, because nobody lines up two players against the quarterback's hips for anything
else. The push trades disguise for force, and over one yard, force wins far more often than not.

### How it became legal: assisting the runner

For most of the NFL's history, the tush push was illegal. The rule on
[**assisting the runner**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-assisting-the-runner) said teammates could
not push or pull a ball carrier forward, a 10-yard foul. In the mid-2000s (accounts differ by a year) the
NFL removed "push" from the rule and kept the ban on *pulling*. The reason was practical: in a pile, officials could never tell who was pushing whom (a runner, a teammate
in contact with the runner, the pile itself), so the rule was close to unenforceable. As Mike Pereira,
another former officiating chief, put it, pushing "became really too difficult to officiate," so the
league simply made it legal.[^push2005] Pulling is still a
foul: a teammate who grabs the runner's arm or jersey and hauls him forward costs his team 10 yards. Watch
for it in a tush-push pile. The college rulebook followed in 2013.[^ncaa]

The timing carries a footnote of its own. On October 15, 2005, USC's Matt Leinart scored the winning
touchdown at Notre Dame with running back Reggie Bush shoving him across the goal line from behind, the
"Bush Push." College rules still banned pushing then, no flag was thrown, and the play became a legend:
the illegal, unforgettable ancestor of a play that is now legal in the NFL.[^bushpush]

For more than 15 years after the change, NFL teams pushed runners only in passing, as piles formed. Then
the Philadelphia Eagles turned it into a designed play.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles, 2022–2025"}
Starting in 2022, Philadelphia ran the push more often and more reliably than anyone had, with the right
ingredients: Jalen Hurts, a quarterback with exceptional leg strength; center Jason Kelce, small for a
center but famously quick off the ball and low; an elite line around him, including right tackle Lane
Johnson; and line coach Jeff Stoutland (with the Eagles through 2025), who drilled the timing. On 1 yard to go, FTN's charters
flagged `{python} pct(USE.loc["PHI"])` of the Eagles' 2022–2025 snaps as quarterback sneaks or pushes,
against a league median of `{python} pct(USE_MED)`; counting every Hurts carry with a yard or less to go,
nflverse has him converting `{python} pct(HURTS[1])` of `{python} HURTS[0]` tries.[^phi] Kelce retired after
the 2023 season; Cam Jurgens, a guard in 2023, took over at center in 2024, and the play kept
working.[^jurgens] Hurts scored the first touchdown of Super Bowl LIX
(February 2025, a 40–22 win over Kansas City) on a tush push.[^lix] **What to notice:** the snap. The
Eagles' line moves as one at the exact instant of the snap, and the defensive linemen are already being
driven back before they have risen out of their stances. The push from behind finishes a play that the
line's timing has mostly won already. (The Eagles' push as a talent and coaching advantage, and how it
compares with the rest of the league, is the subject of
[The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd).)
:::

### The ban debate

The push's success made it controversial. Critics made three arguments: **safety** (a pile of the
heaviest players on the field driving forward with heads down), **aesthetics** (a near-automatic yard
is dull football), and **fairness** (one team's mastery of a play is a reason to rethink it). Defenders
of the play answered that injuries on it were rare, that other teams could copy it, and that you don't
ban a play for being executed well.

In 2025 Green Bay proposed a ban. Its first version, barring teammates from pushing the quarterback
immediately at the snap, was tabled at the spring league meeting; a broader revision, barring any pushing,
pulling, lifting or assisting of the runner except by blocking opponents, came to a vote on May 21, 2025, and **failed
22–10**, two votes short of the 24 needed (rule changes need three-quarters of the 32 owners). The league
tightened its officiating guidance instead. In practice that meant watching for linemen who move before the
snap (a false start, easy to miss when everyone is crouched shoulder to shoulder) and for players lined up
in or across the neutral zone, the ball-length strip between the two lines; the officiating department's
own training video in September 2025 said an Eagles guard should have been flagged for moving early on one
push.[^poe] For
2026, **no team proposed a ban**; the competition committee's co-chairman said in February 2026 that he
didn't expect one, and the league said it would only "lightly" revisit how the play is officiated. The
tush push is legal for the 2026 season.[^ban]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The tush push is unstoppable." It isn't, and the next section's numbers show that. Defenses stop it by
winning the snap: crowding both A gaps beside the center, timing the count so their linemen are moving
first, and sending linebackers over the top to meet the quarterback before the pile moves. (Leaping over
the pile is legal on a running play; many fans assume it isn't.[^leap]) Defensive linemen also try to jump
the snap count, accepting the occasional offside penalty for the chance of getting into the backfield
early. What the push does is shift the odds of a one-yard contest, and on one yard that shift is worth a
great deal.
:::

### Does it work? The sneak in the data

FTN's charting service marks every play it thinks was a quarterback sneak (`is_qb_sneak`), and the flag
covers the plain sneak and the push alike, because FTN does not chart them separately. So the numbers
below are for sneaks of every kind.[^ftnflag]

On 1 yard to go, 2022–2025 regular seasons, sneaks gained the first down or the touchdown
`{python} pct(SN_RATE)` of the time (`{python} f"{SN_N:,}"` plays). Other runs on 1 yard to go converted
`{python} pct(RUN_RATE)`, and passes `{python} pct(PAS_RATE)`. A gap of
`{python} f"{(SN_RATE - RUN_RATE) * 100:.0f}"` percentage points on a play
that decides whether a drive lives is an enormous difference. With 2 yards to go, sneaks were far rarer and
far less successful (`{python} pct(SN2["conv"].mean())` of `{python} len(SN2)`), which tells you what the
play is for: the last yard, not the last two. A sneak is a pile moving forward, and a pile of a dozen big
men moves a yard, maybe a yard and a half, before it stalls (watch the frame strip above). Ask it for two
and it usually stops short.

You have now met three numbers for "one yard": sneaks from the 1 scored on
`{python} pct(TD1.loc["sneak", "mean"])` of plays, sneaks on any 1-yard-to-go snap converted
`{python} pct(SN_RATE)`, and drives with first-and-goal at the 1 scored `{python} pct(FG_TD.loc[1, "mean"])`
of the time. They measure different things. The drive number is highest because a drive gets up to four
tries at the yard. And the yard before the goal line is harder than the yard before a first down: there the
defense's back line is the goal line itself, so it can put every defender within a few yards of the ball,
and it brings in its goal-line personnel to do it. In the middle of the field, a defense crowding the line on
third-and-1 still has to worry about a pass over its head.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sneak-teams
#| fig-cap: "Quarterback sneaks (including tush pushes) on 1 or 2 yards to go, by team, 2022–2025 regular seasons. Left: how many each team ran. Right: the share that gained a first down or a touchdown, with a bar showing the range that chance alone could easily produce (a 90% interval) around each team's rate; teams with fewer than 15 attempts are left out of the right panel. The dashed line is the league rate. Philadelphia (blue) ran far more than anyone; Buffalo (orange) was second. Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (is_qb_sneak)."
T = TEAM.sort_values("n", ascending=True)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.2), sharey=True, gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.25]})
ypos = np.arange(len(T))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if t == "PHI" else (style.SERIES[1] if t == "BUF" else style.BASELINE) for t in T.index]
axes[0].barh(ypos, T["n"], color=cols, height=0.7)
for y, n in zip(ypos, T["n"]):
    axes[0].text(n + 2, y, f"{n}", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2)
axes[0].set_yticks(ypos)
axes[0].set_yticklabels(T.index, fontsize=6.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Sneaks run", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("How many", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_xlim(0, T["n"].max() * 1.18)
axes[0].grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ok = T["n"] >= 15
se = np.sqrt(T["rate"] * (1 - T["rate"]) / T["n"])
for y, (t, row), s, c, keep in zip(ypos, T.iterrows(), se, cols, ok):
    if not keep:
        continue
    lo, hi = max(0, row["rate"] - 1.645 * s), min(1, row["rate"] + 1.645 * s)
    axes[1].plot([lo * 100, hi * 100], [y, y], color=c if c != style.BASELINE else style.MUTED, lw=1.4,
                 alpha=0.6)
    axes[1].plot([row["rate"] * 100], [y], marker="o", ms=5, color=c if c != style.BASELINE else style.INK_2)
axes[1].axvline(SN12_RATE * 100, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
axes[1].text(SN12_RATE * 100 + 0.8, 1.0, f"league\n{SN12_RATE * 100:.0f}%", fontsize=6.8,
             color=style.INK_2, va="center")
axes[1].set_xlim(45, 102)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Converted (first down or TD), %", fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("How often it worked", fontsize=9)
axes[1].grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

Two lessons hide in that chart. First, **volume, not rate, is what separates the teams**. Most teams'
conversion rates overlap once you account for sample size: 40 sneaks is not enough to tell an 80% team
from an 85% team. What differs enormously is how often teams *call* the play. The Eagles stand
alone at one end; at the other, Kansas City was charted with `{python} int(TEAM.loc["KC", "n"])` in four
seasons, because Andy Reid's offense almost never asks Patrick Mahomes to sneak.

If the sneak converts that often, why don't the other teams run it more? None of the reasons is foolish.
The sneak puts the quarterback, usually the most valuable and most expensive player on the roster, at the
bottom of a pile of the biggest men on the field. Many modern offenses live in the shotgun, so their
quarterback rarely takes a snap under center, and the sneak is a play they would have to practise
specially. And the play needs a line that can win the first half-second together, which not every team
has. A coach weighing a few extra yards a season against those costs can reasonably say no.

Second, **a high rate is partly selection**. Teams sneak when the distance is truly short, often inches
rather than a full yard (the play-by-play records both as "1 to go"), and most teams sneak only when they
like the look. That explains a puzzle you may have noticed. The push adds hundreds of pounds of force, yet
Philadelphia's sneak rate in the chart sits close to the league line, and Hurts's mark in the film room is
no better than Brady's or Allen's on their own. The Eagles called the play on about half of all their
1-yard downs: on full yards as well as inches, against defenses that knew it was coming and lined up to stop
it. Other teams sneaked only when the spot and the look were good. Comparing the two rates compares a play
run every time with a play run only when it was easy, which is why the Eagles' rate is more impressive than
it looks. How much the push really adds once you account for that is a harder question, taken up in
[the Eagles case study](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd).

## Putting it together: a red-zone possession

Here is how the pieces fit on one drive. First-and-10 at the opponent's 18: the defense still has some
depth to protect, so you'll see two-high safeties, zone coverage and the offense's normal playbook. A
completion to the 7 makes it first-and-goal, and the picture changes: the safeties come down, the corners
press, and the coverage is mostly man. The offense answers with quick throws: a slant or a fade on the
outside if it likes a matchup, a rub from a bunch if it sees man, a sprint-out if it wants an easy read.
Inside the 3, both teams change personnel: jumbo against goal-line defense. Now it's a run, a quarterback
sneak or push, or the play-action pass that the heavy personnel sets up. And if the drive ends in a
touchdown, there's one more decision: kick, or one more play from the 2.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: fade or rub?"}
*When the ball crosses the 20*

- Count the safeties. Two deep at the 18 is normal; one or none inside the 10 means the defense has
  traded depth for bodies near the ball.
- Look at the corners' depth. A corner a yard off the receiver is pressing: expect man coverage.

*Inside the 10: read the receivers' splits*

- **A receiver alone, wide, with 5 to 8 yards to the sideline?** That spacing is for a fade or back-shoulder
  throw. Check the corner's leverage: lined up inside him, think fade; outside him, think slant.
- **Receivers bunched or stacked, tight to the formation?** That's rub territory. Predict a crossing
  pattern against man, and watch whether the defenders switch (banjo) or chase through the traffic.
- **The quarterback in the gun with receivers flooded to one side?** Look for a sprint-out to that side.

*Inside the 3*

- Heavy personnel on both sides? Watch the quarterback: under center with players stacked directly behind
  him is a tush push; a fullback and tailback deep behind him is a handoff or play-action.
- On the push, watch the snap and the first half-second, not the pile: whichever line fires first and lower
  usually wins.

*After a touchdown*

- If the offense stays on the field, guess the concept before the snap from its formation: bunch (rub),
  spread with a back beside the quarterback (QB run or sprint-out), or heavy (run or play-action).

For your prediction log ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)): inside the 10, write
one word before each snap, from the splits alone: *fade* (fade or back-shoulder), *rub*, *quick* (slant or
out), *sprint* (sprint-out) or *run*.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the receiver alone"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-iso
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-goal at the opponent's 7. Three receivers to the right, X alone on the left. Read the corner and the safeties before you read the answer."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -19.5), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.0, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -3.5, "W"),
                 D("NB", "NB", 3.5, 9.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 6.5, "SS"),
                 D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.0, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 1.1, -18.3, "CB"),
                 D("FS", "FS", 11.0, 4.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(7), to_go=None)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-26.67, 17.5), window=(-7.0, 17))
goal_marks(fld, p, -9.0)
plt.show()
```

**Where is the ball most likely going, and what would change your answer after the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**To X on the left, most likely a fade.** Everything about the alignment points there. X is alone on his side,
lined up with about 7 yards to the sideline, exactly the room a fade needs. The corner is pressing a yard
off him and lined up a step *inside* him: inside leverage, which takes away the slant and gives up the
outside release. And the safety help has rotated toward the three receivers on the right: the strong safety
has walked over them and the free safety sits in the end zone just outside the right hash, much too far away
to reach a ball thrown toward the left pylon a second after the snap. The three receivers on the right are
there partly to *pull* that help away. Coaches call this a "backside" or isolation fade.

**What would change it:** if the corner ran with X stride for stride over the top, the better throw is the
back-shoulder: thrown early, behind X's outside shoulder, and caught a yard or two deep in the end zone. If
the corner had lined up outside X, the slant would be open instead. And if the free safety had stayed in the
middle or shaded left, the quarterback would likely work the three-receiver side, where the defense would
then be short a man.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: call the two-point play"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-twopoint
#| fig-cap: "A two-point try from the 2. The offense is in the shotgun with two receivers on each side and the running back beside the quarterback. The defense has brought in six defensive backs: one on each receiver, pressed or close, and two safeties standing in the end zone. Count the defenders in the box between the tight ends' spots, within five yards of the ball."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.5, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.0),
                 O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.0, 0.5, "M"),
                 D("LCB", "CB", 1.0, -14.4, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.6, -8.4, "$"),
                 D("DB", "DB", 1.6, 8.4, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.0, 14.4, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 5.6, -6.8, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 5.6, 6.8, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(2), to_go=None)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 19.0), window=(-7.0, 12))
x0, y0 = P(fld, p, 5.0, -4.6)
x1, y1 = P(fld, p, -0.2, 4.6)
fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=style.MUTED, alpha=0.08,
                           ec=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))
say(fld, p, 5.7, 0.0, "the box", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, box=False)
plt.show()
```

**You have the four shapes from the two-point figure (A–D) on your call sheet. Which one do you call
against this look, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**D, the quarterback run (QB power), with the sprint-out option (C) as the second choice.** Count the box:
four linemen and one linebacker, five defenders. Count your blockers on a quarterback run: five linemen
plus the running back, six, and the quarterback carries the ball. That is one more blocker than the box has
defenders, the extra-hat arithmetic, and the two safeties are standing three or four yards deep in the end
zone, so the runner needs only two yards before they arrive. The defense has bet everything on stopping a
pass: a defender on every receiver and two more behind them. The bunch rub (A) and the snag (B) would throw
into that bet.

**What would change it:** a safety walking down into the box before the snap (or, harder to see, timing his
run to arrive at the snap). Then the count is even and the pass becomes the better bet, because a defender
has left the coverage. That trade, the defense guessing and the offense counting, is the whole two-point
game. Most defenses avoid this look for exactly this reason: on the 2023–2025 two-point tries in the
participation data, they had six or seven defenders in the box on `{python} pct(TP_BOX67)` of them.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: second-and-goal at the 1"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-goalline
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-goal at the opponent's 1. On first down the offense ran an iso from this same formation and was stopped short. Same personnel on both sides: the offense in 23 personnel (Y and U on the line, H as a wing, the fullback and running back stacked behind the quarterback under center); the defense in its 6-2 goal-line defense. This time its three defensive backs have crept up close to the line."
dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -6.0, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -3.9, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.85, "T"),
       D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.85, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 3.9, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 6.3, "E"),
       D("LB1", "LB", 2.6, -2.3, "M"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.6, 2.3, "W"),
       D("CB1", "CB", 1.8, -7.4, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 1.8, 8.2, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 2.8, 5.0, "SS")]
p = Play(jumbo(), dfn, los=opp(1), to_go=None)
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.2, lateral=(-10.5, 10.5), window=(-8.0, 7.0))
say(fld, p, 5.0, -5.0, "end zone", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
plt.show()
```

**The defense has packed everyone in to stop the run. What call makes it pay, and which offensive player
should you watch?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Play-action from the same look.** The quarterback fakes the iso to the running back behind the fullback;
the line fires out exactly as it did on first down, so every defender's eyes go to the pile. Then a tight
end who seemed to be blocking slips into the end zone: Y or U blocks for a count and releases, or the wing,
H, leaks to the corner of the end zone. Watch **the backside tight end, U**. On a run he blocks the end in
front of him; on play-action he chips the end and releases, and the defensive back responsible for him,
crept up to help against the run, is the one who has to see it.

This is exactly what goal-line offenses do. Inside the 3 in 2023–2025, offenses with one wide receiver or
none passed on only `{python} pct(HEAVY_PASS)` of snaps, but `{python} pct(HEAVY_PA)` of those passes came
off a run fake. **What could go wrong:** a defense in a 5-3 has an extra linebacker standing up who can see
the release, and a quarterback under center who fakes and turns his back has very little time against a
front built to get into the backfield. One more run is never a bad answer either; the threat of the pass is
what keeps those three defensive backs honest.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Near the goal line the **end line becomes the deepest defender**. The compressed field squeezes zones,
  frees safeties to come down, and makes man coverage, press and Cover 0 cheap. The offense loses its deep
  threat, and every throw arrives into a crowd.
- Red-zone pass concepts win quickly and close: the **fade** and **back-shoulder throw** against press with no
  outside help, the **slant** when the corner takes away the fade, **rubs** from stacks and bunches against
  man, the **shovel pass** against an attacking front, and the **sprint-out** that puts a flat defender in
  conflict.
- A good **two-point play** gives the offense two answers that put one defender in conflict, so it works
  against more than one defensive call. Runs have converted more often than passes since 2015, partly
  because of who chooses to run, and a try is worth about what the kick is, so the scoreboard decides.
- **Goal-line defenses** (6-2, 5-3) trade defensive backs for linemen and linebackers and fill every gap;
  low man wins. Their weakness is the play that looks like the run and isn't, which is why heavy personnel
  that throws near the goal line almost always fakes a run first.
- The **QB sneak** is the best one-yard play in football: the ball starts closest to the line, the play is
  instant, and the quarterback-as-runner adds a blocker. The **tush push** adds pushers behind him; it has
  been legal since the NFL removed the ban on pushing the runner in the **mid-2000s** (2005 or 2006; pulling is still a foul),
  survived a **22–10 ban vote in 2025**, and is legal in **2026**.
- In the data, a little under six red-zone trips in ten end in touchdowns; a first-and-goal from the 1 scores
  about nine times in ten (a drive gets four tries); and sneaks convert about four in five on 1 yard to go,
  but only about half the time on 2. Teams differ far more in how often they sneak than in how well, and the
  teams that sneak most face the hardest looks.

**From simulation to real tracking data.** The two animations in this chapter (the rub and the tush push) are gridiron simulations
written in NFL Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) has
every player's position ten times a second, before and after the snap, so you can find real quarterback
sneaks and tush pushes (the Eagles ran plenty in those weeks) and draw them with the same code. The data lives
on Kaggle and needs your own free login, so this cell is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
# short-yardage quarterback runs: 1 yard to go, play description names the quarterback up the middle
sneaks = plays[(plays["yardsToGo"] <= 1)
               & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("up the middle|sneak", case=False, na=False)
               & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("Hurts|Allen", na=False)]
print(len(sneaks), "candidate sneaks")
g, pl = sneaks.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[-0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5])   # same call as the simulated plays
```
:::

[^twohigh]: This book's calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` joined to play-by-play: regular-season dropbacks, 2023–2025 (all charted by FTN, one source), with a charted `defense_coverage_type`, excluding BLOWN, COMBO and PREVENT, and excluding COVER_9, which staffs use both for a rotated Cover 3 and for split-field calls, so it belongs to neither group. Two-deep = COVER_2, 2_MAN, COVER_4 and COVER_6. "Outside the red zone" = more than 20 yards from the goal line. Coverage labels are a charter's judgment, and the 2018–2022 (NGS) labels are coded differently, so the comparison is kept within one source.

[^rz]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`fixed_drive_result`), 2022–2025 regular seasons: every drive with at least one scrimmage run or pass (not a kneel-down, extra point or two-point try) snapped at the opponent's 20 or closer, counted once. Tries are left out because the extra point is snapped from the 15 and the two-point try from the 2, so counting them would turn every touchdown into a "red-zone trip". The rest: turnovers `{python} pct(RZ_SHARE.get("Turnover", 0), 1)`, turnovers on downs `{python} pct(RZ_SHARE.get("Turnover on downs", 0), 1)`, missed field goals `{python} pct(RZ_SHARE.get("Missed field goal", 0), 1)`, the end of a half `{python} pct(RZ_SHARE.get("End of half", 0), 1)`, and a handful of turnovers returned for touchdowns and punts.

[^passrate]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2022–2025 regular seasons: dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles) as a share of runs and dropbacks on first to third down, with the offense's win probability between 10% and 90% and more than two minutes left in the half.

[^fromone]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, 2022–2025 regular seasons, every run or dropback snapped from the opponent's 1 (kneel-downs excluded). Sneaks are plays FTN flags `is_qb_sneak`; dropbacks include sacks and scrambles. Sample sizes: `{python} int(TD1.loc["sneak", "size"])` sneaks, `{python} int(TD1.loc["run", "size"])` other runs and `{python} int(TD1.loc["dropback", "size"])` dropbacks.

[^ezthrows]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2022–2025 regular seasons, passes thrown from the opponent's 10 or closer (sacks excluded). "Into the end zone" = air yards at least the distance to the goal line; "toward the outside" = the scorer's `pass_location` left or right. Touchdowns per throw from `pass_touchdown`; interceptions per throw were `{python} pct(EZ_INT, 1)` for the end-zone throws and `{python} pct(SHORT_INT, 1)` for the short ones. Two-point tries are excluded. The data cannot identify the route, so this group includes corner routes and other throws as well as fades and back-shoulder throws.

[^scoring]: *Official Playing Rules of the National Football League* (2026), Rule 11, Section 2 (a touchdown is scored when the ball is on, above or behind the opponent's goal line while legally in possession of a runner) and Rule 8, Section 1, Article 3 (a completed catch: control, both feet or another body part down in bounds, then an act common to the game): <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/> . Both are taught in [The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) and [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd).

[^heavy]: This book's calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` (charted personnel) joined to play-by-play and FTN charting (`is_play_action`), 2023–2025 regular seasons: runs and dropbacks snapped from the opponent's 3 or closer, kneel-downs and two-point tries excluded. "Heavy" = at most one wide receiver on the field (`offense_personnel`); dropbacks include sacks and scrambles.

[^jurgens]: NFL.com, "Eagles' Nick Sirianni: Cam Jurgens did 'really nice job' replacing legend Jason Kelce" (2024 season): <https://www.nfl.com/news/eagles-nick-sirianni-cam-jurgens-really-nice-job-replacing-legend-jason-kelce> .

[^poe]: Jonathan Jones, "NFL instructs refs to keep eagle eye on Tush Push, QB sneaks after controversial Week 2," CBS Sports (September 18, 2025): officials instructed "to ensure the offensive linemen are not lining up in the neutral zone," and the training video covered false starts and offensive offside on the play: <https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-instructs-refs-to-keep-eagle-eye-on-tush-push-qb-sneaks-after-controversial-week-2> ; Rob Maaddi, "NFL: Eagles should've been penalized for a false start on a tush-push conversion vs. the Chiefs," Associated Press (September 19, 2025), quoting Ramon George, the NFL's vice president of officiating training and development: "Prior to the snap, looks like we have movement by the right guard": <https://www.wsls.com/sports/2025/09/19/nfl-eagles-shouldve-been-penalized-for-a-false-start-on-a-tush-push-conversion-vs-the-chiefs/> .

Down, distance, clock (0:26 at the snap) and Seattle's one remaining timeout: nflverse play-by-play (game 2014_21). Three wide receivers, New England's goal-line personnel and Carroll's reasoning ("When [the Patriots] sent their goal-line guys in, I know we have the advantage on the matchups in the passing game"; the throw depended on "how we had to save the clock to get in all of our plays"): Terry Blount, ESPN, February 3, 2015, via ABC7: <https://abc7.com/post/carroll-throwing-was-part-of-the-plan/501284/> . Butler's quote on the stacked receivers: *Boston Globe*, February 2, 2015: <https://www.bostonglobe.com/sports/football/2015/02/02/name-decides-super-bowl-malcolm-butler-does-job/LiVP49K7LDfMK9PwuyKylJ/story.html> .

[^shovel]: Kansas City 27, Philadelphia 20, September 17, 2017 (Week 2), Arrowhead Stadium; Kelce's 15-yard shovel-pass touchdown on second down from the Philadelphia 15 with 6:32 left broke a 13–13 tie: Pro Football Reference box score, <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201709170kan.htm> , and nflverse play-by-play; Fox 29, "Kansas City Chiefs, Andy Reid beat Eagles 27-20": <https://www.fox29.com/news/kansas-city-chiefs-andy-reid-beat-eagles-27-20> .

[^twopt]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "2-point conversion turns 30 years old" (the AFL used it 1960–1969; the NFL adopted it in 1994; Tom Tupa scored the first one): <https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2024/09/2-point-conversion-turns-30-years-old> ; CBS Sports, "NFL rule change: Extra point moved back, defenses can score" (2015: extra-point snap moved to the 15, defense may return a failed try for two points): <https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-rule-change-extra-point-moved-back-defenses-can-score> . The try is snapped from the 2 in the NFL and the 3 in college: Wikipedia, "Two-point conversion": <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-point_conversion> . No change to the two-point spot was proposed for 2026.

[^tpdef]: This book's calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` joined to play-by-play, 2023–2025 regular seasons: two-point tries recorded as a run or a pass (`{python} TP_N3` plays). "Defensive backs" = cornerbacks plus safeties in the charted `defense_personnel`. Man coverage = COVER_0, COVER_1 or 2_MAN, among dropbacks with a charted coverage (BLOWN, COMBO and PREVENT excluded).

[^twodata]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2015–2025 regular seasons: two-point tries (`two_point_attempt`) whose play was recorded as a run or a pass, success from `two_point_conv_result`. Scrambles and sacks count as passes. Tries erased by penalties are left out. The extra-point rate is every regular-season kick from 2015 to 2025 (`extra_point_result` "good").

[^li]: Super Bowl LI, February 5, 2017, NRG Stadium, Houston: New England 34, Atlanta 28 (OT). Fourth-quarter conversions: James White on a direct snap after Amendola's 6-yard touchdown catch (28–20, 5:56 left); Brady to Amendola after White's 1-yard touchdown run (28–28, 0:57 left): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LI> ; times from nflverse play-by-play (game 2016_21). The direct snap (Brady in the shotgun, White motioning beside him; the Patriots' "Ride 34 Direct", the call Kevin Faulk had scored a two-point try on in Super Bowl XXXVIII): ESPN's breakdown of both tries: <https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/18628898/how-new-england-patriots-converted-two-point-tries-super-bowl-li> ; *Concord Monitor*: <https://www.concordmonitor.com/?p=201569> .

[^ineligible]: *Official Playing Rules of the National Football League* (2026), Rule 8, Section 3, Article 1: "On a scrimmage play during which a legal forward pass is thrown, it is a foul if the entire body of an ineligible offensive player ... is more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass has been thrown," unless he got there while blocking an opponent he engaged within a yard of the line; 5 yards: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/> . The NCAA allows linemen up to 3 yards downfield and exempts passes caught behind the line: Wikipedia, "Ineligible receiver downfield": <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineligible_receiver_downfield> .

[^leap]: *Official Playing Rules of the National Football League* (2026), Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1(r): the leaping foul is "running forward and leaping across the line of scrimmage in an obvious attempt to block a field goal or Try Kick, or apparent kick"; no rule restricts leaping on a running play: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/> .

[^fridge]: Super Bowl XX, January 26, 1986, Louisiana Superdome, New Orleans: Chicago 46, New England 10; Perry's 1-yard touchdown run came late in the third quarter and made it 44–3: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XX> ; NFL.com, "100 Greatest Plays": <https://nfl.com/100/originals/100-greatest/plays-79> .

[^qbone]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2000–2022, regular season and playoffs: runs with Tom Brady as the ball carrier on 1 yard (or less) to go, kneel-downs excluded; "converted" = first down or touchdown. Most (about 83%) were logged as runs up the middle, the sneak's signature; the rest went just left or right of center.

[^push2005]: Pereira (speaking in 2022) quoted in Ben Volin, "NFL saves the Tush Push — for now — but could revert to old rule to ban all pushing plays instead," *Boston Globe* (April 2, 2025): <https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/04/02/sports/nfl-tush-push-rule/> . The 2006 date: Joel Bussert, NFL historian, quoted in Cliff Christl, "Would the 1906 rule changes banning the 'Turtle-Back Wedge' apply to the 'Tush Push'?", Packers.com (May 1, 2025): <https://www.packers.com/news/would-the-1906-rule-changes-banning-the-turtle-back-wedge-apply-to-the-tush-push> , and Dean Blandino on Fox (via Fox News, 2025): <https://www.foxnews.com/sports/dean-blandino-its-50-50-tush-push-survives-eagles-chiefs-controversies.amp> . The 2005 date and the old 10-yard foul: Doug Robinson, *Deseret News* (January 20, 2023), as cited in Wikipedia, "Tush Push": <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tush_Push> ; Kevin Seifert, "Vote on tush push ban tabled by NFL owners for more discussion," ESPN (April 1, 2025), which gives both 2004 and 2005: <https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/44490292/sources-tush-push-ban-vote-tabled-nfl-owners> . Current rule: *Official Playing Rules of the National Football League* (2026), Rule 12, Section 1, Article 4, "Assisting the runner": no offensive player may "pull a runner in any direction at any time"; loss of 10 yards: <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/> .

[^ncaa]: Kyle Bonagura, "The legacy and legality of the Bush Push 20 years later," ESPN (October 15, 2025): the NCAA rule on helping the ball carrier kept its ban on pushing until 2013, when "push" was removed: <https://africa.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/46592420/reggie-bush-push-usc-notre-dame-rivalry-legacy-20-years-later-2025> .

[^bushpush]: USC won 34–31 at Notre Dame on October 15, 2005; USC trailed 31–28 with seven seconds left before Leinart's sneak. Bonagura (ESPN, 2025, cited above) on the play being illegal under the college rule of the time, and unflagged.

[^phi]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, 2022–2025 regular seasons: share of each team's runs and dropbacks on 1 yard to go flagged `is_qb_sneak` (kneel-downs excluded). Hurts: nflverse play-by-play, 2020–2025, regular season and playoffs, runs with Jalen Hurts as the ball carrier for Philadelphia on 1 yard or less to go, kneel-downs excluded.

[^lix]: Super Bowl LIX, February 9, 2025, Caesars Superdome, New Orleans: Philadelphia 40, Kansas City 22; Hurts's first-quarter touchdown on the tush push: <https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/nfl-mvp-super-bowl-jalen-hurts-eagles> .

[^ban]: The first version's wording ("would prohibit an offensive player from immediately pushing a teammate who is lined up directly behind the snapper and receives the snap") and the April 1, 2025 tabling: Kevin Seifert, ESPN (cited above). The revised version ("pushing, pulling, lifting, or assisting the runner except by individually blocking opponents for him") and its 22–10 failure on May 21, 2025: *SI*, "Packers' proposal to ban Eagles' tush push fails again": <https://www.si.com/nfl/packers/packers-proposal-to-ban-eagles-tush-push-fails-again> , and *Philadelphia Inquirer*: <https://www.inquirer.com/eagles/eagles-tush-push-packers-ban-vote-20250519.html> ; no proposal for 2026 and McKay's comments: NFL.com, <https://www.nfl.com/news/competition-committee-co-chairman-rich-mckay-doesn-t-expect-tush-push-ban-proposal-in-2026> ; Troy Vincent on revisiting officiating "lightly": *The Washington Times* (Feb. 24, 2026), <https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/feb/24/nfl-receives-no-tush-push-ban-proposal-year-effort-last-year-ban/> .

[^ftnflag]: FTN charting via nflverse `load_ftn_charting()` (2022 onward). FTN's data dictionary has no separate tush-push flag; `is_qb_sneak` covers both: <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html> . The sneak rates here count plays FTN flagged and nflverse recorded as runs, on 1 (or 2) yards to go, 2022–2025 regular seasons; "converted" = first down or touchdown on the play. Other runs exclude scrambles and kneel-downs; passes include sacks and scrambles. By season, sneaks on 1 yard to go converted `{python} ", ".join(f"{pct(v)} ({int(s)})" for s, v in SN_SEASON.items())`.

[^qballen]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2018–2025, regular season and playoffs: runs with Josh Allen as the ball carrier for Buffalo on 1 yard or less to go, kneel-downs excluded; "converted" = first down or touchdown. Team sneak counts: FTN `is_qb_sneak`, as in the chart.
